quote: Wie viel n Ecke giebt es, die nicht continuir- lich in einander übergeführt werden können
english: How many n-gons are there that cannot be continuously transformed into one another?
topic: A list of research tasks: counting n-gons that cannot be continuously deformed into one another, proving that the Plücker formulas and Klein's reality formulas suffice as relations among the ordinary singularities of a curve, proving finiteness of invariants for subgroups of continuous linear transformations, and defining 'Geschlechtszahlen' of a form via representations by its partial derivatives.

triage.modern_statement: One plausible reading: classify closed planar polygons with n vertices, possibly self-intersecting, up to continuous deformation through non-degenerate n-gons, and count the resulting classes (the connected components of the space of such n-gons). If 'deformation' means regular homotopy (every intermediate polygon stays a regular closed polygon), this is the polygonal version of the Whitney–Graustein classification of closed curves by turning number. For an n-gon the turning number is restricted by n; for example, the star polygon {n/k} has turning number k with k < n/2. If simple (embedded) polygons were meant, the question is instead about the connectedness of the space of simple n-gons. The note does not say which equivalence Hilbert intended.
triage.answered_by: No historical answer to Hilbert's note was found. Under the regular-homotopy reading, the answer follows from the discrete (polygonal) Whitney–Graustein theorem: regular closed polygons are classified up to regular homotopy by their tangent winding (turning) number. The smooth theorem is due to Whitney (1937), building on Graustein; the polygonal version is presented, for example, in TU Berlin discrete differential geometry course material (2013). I could not find a source tying this specifically to Hilbert, and I could not confirm the exact count as a function of n.

evidence.claim: Course material on the discrete Whitney–Graustein theorem defines a regular homotopy between planar closed polygons as a continuous path of regular closed polygons. It then proves the polygonal Whitney–Graustein theorem, using turning angles summing to 2πm, i.e. classification by the tangent winding number m.

Spaces of planar n-gons, including simple polygons and polygons degenerated to segments, are still studied as topological objects. For example, a 2024 paper notes that degenerate n-gons lie in the boundary of the space of simple polygons.
The topology of planar polygon spaces with fixed side lengths (Betti numbers and similar invariants) is also an established research topic, though it is a different problem from Hilbert's question.

triage.why: The note is a one-line question and does not specify the equivalence. Isotopy of simple polygons, regular homotopy of possibly self-intersecting polygons, and other notions of deformation give different problems. It is not among Hilbert's 23 published problems or the 24th problem, and I found no source discussing this diary entry. Under the most natural reading (regular homotopy), the polygonal Whitney–Graustein theorem settles it: classes correspond to the turning numbers an n-gon can realize. A tool limit cut my search short, so I could not cite a source for the exact allowed range of turning numbers or for the simple-polygon reading. Spaces of polygons remain a research topic, but I cannot say whether Hilbert's specific counting question is pursued today.
